slides.body: Every run step is a new shell process started from a documented command template, so state survives a step only if it's written to a file the runner provides …

slides.headline: The shell, precisely
slides.body: The runner writes your run text to a temporary script file and executes it with a template in which a placeholder stands for that file.

slides.direction: The template table of section 20A.7.

slides.caption: If you write nothing on Windows: PowerShell Core.

slides.direction: Draw three boxes in a row, one per step, and label each "new shell process". Then draw the file underneath, with the first step appending to it and the later steps reading through the `steps` context. Last, the job boundary on the right.
slides.text:
JOB build (one runner, one filesystem)
  +----------------------+   +----------------------+   +----------------------+
  | step id=describe     |   | step                 |   | step id=list         |
  | new shell process    |   | new shell process    |   | new shell process    |
  | export X=1  (lost)   |   | X is empty           |   |                      |
  | cd build    (lost)   |   | back in workspace    |   |                      |
  +----------+-----------+   +-----------^----------+   +----------+-----------+
             | echo "describe=..." >>    | ${{ steps.describe      | echo "files=..." >>
             v "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"          |     .outputs.describe }}v "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
  ==========================================================================================
   GITHUB_OUTPUT: an append-only file per step; the runner reads it when the step ends
  ==========================================================================================
             |
             |  jobs.build.outputs:  describe, files        (strings only)
             v
  JOB report (another runner):  env: DESCRIBE: ${{ needs.build.outputs.describe }}
                                run: echo "$DESCRIBE"

beats.text: A nightly evaluation job has been green for three weeks. Someone opens the saved report by chance and finds failing tests in it, from the first of those nights on. The step ran the tests and piped their output into tee, a program that copies what it receives into a file, to keep a copy of the log. A pipe is the vertical bar that feeds one command's output to the next. The tests failed. tee succeeded. The step was green.
beats.tele: A nightly evaluation job has been green for three weeks. Someone opens the saved report by chance and finds failing tests in it, from the first of those nights on. A pipe is the vertical bar that feeds one command's output to the next. The tests failed. `tee` succeeded. The step was green.

beats.tele: In one sentence. Every `run` step is a new shell process started from a documented command template, so state survives a step only if it's written to a file the runner provides: `GITHUB_OUTPUT` for named outputs, `GITHUB_ENV` for environment variables, `GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` for a report.

beats.text: The shell, precisely. The runner writes your run text to a temporary script file and executes it with a template in which a placeholder stands for that file.
beats.tele: The shell, precisely. The runner writes your `run` text to a temporary script file and executes it with a template in which a placeholder stands for that file.

beats.text: If you write nothing, on Linux or macOS, the runner executes bash -e with the file.
beats.tele: If you write nothing, on Linux or macOS, the runner executes `bash -e` with the file.

beats.text: If you write shell: bash, on any platform, it executes bash --noprofile --norc -eo pipefail with the file.
beats.tele: If you write `shell: bash`, on any platform, it executes `bash --noprofile --norc -eo pipefail` with the file.

beats.text: If you write nothing on Windows: PowerShell Core.
beats.tele: If you write nothing on Windows: PowerShell Core.

beats.text: If you write nothing inside a job container on Linux: sh, not bash.
beats.tele: If you write nothing inside a job container on Linux: `sh`, not `bash`.

beats.text: And shell: python runs the file with Python.
beats.tele: And `shell: python` runs the file with Python.

beats.text: Quick quiz, with the table still in front of you. On a Linux runner, bash already runs your script. You add shell: bash to the step. Does anything change? A, nothing. B, the shell's options. Your answer?
beats.tele: Quick quiz, with the table still in front of you. On a Linux runner, bash already runs your script. You add `shell: bash` to the step. Does anything change? A, nothing. B, the shell's options. Your answer?

beats.text: B, the options change. Look at the first two rows again, because they're the hook. Both have -e. Only the second has pipefail.
beats.tele: B, the options change. Look at the first two rows again, because they're the hook. Both have `-e`. Only the second has `pipefail`.

beats.text: -e stops the script at the first command that fails, that is, a command that returns an exit status other than zero. It doesn't look inside a pipeline. The status of a pipeline is the status of its last command, unless pipefail is set. So the implicit default lets a failing test command piped into tee pass.
beats.tele: `-e` stops the script at the first command that fails, that is, a command that returns an exit status other than zero. It doesn't look inside a pipeline. The status of a pipeline is the status of its last command, unless `pipefail` is set. So the implicit default lets a failing test command piped into `tee` pass.

beats.text: The irony is worth saying aloud: writing shell: bash explicitly, which looks like stating the default, changes the behavior. It isn't the default. The default is a weaker invocation of the same program.
beats.tele: The irony is worth saying aloud: writing `shell: bash` explicitly, which looks like stating the default, changes the behavior. It isn't the default. The default is a weaker invocation of the same program.

says: shell: bash looks like the default. The default is a weaker invocation of the same program

beats.text: The files, precisely. The runner creates files and puts their paths in environment variables.
beats.tele: The files, precisely. The runner creates files and puts their paths in environment variables.

beats.text: GITHUB_OUTPUT: you append name=value. The step, which needs an id, then has an output of that name under the steps context. Job outputs are limited to 1 MB per job and 50 MB per run.
beats.tele: `GITHUB_OUTPUT`: you append `name=value`. The step, which needs an `id`, then has an output of that name under the `steps` context. Job outputs are limited to 1 MB per job and 50 MB per run.

beats.text: GITHUB_ENV: you append NAME=value. Later steps of the job get the environment variable. The writing step itself doesn't. And it can't override variables that start with GITHUB_ or RUNNER_.
beats.tele: `GITHUB_ENV`: you append `NAME=value`. Later steps of the job get the environment variable. The writing step itself doesn't. And it can't override variables that start with `GITHUB_` or `RUNNER_`.

beats.text: GITHUB_PATH: you append a directory, and it's prepended to PATH for later steps.
beats.tele: `GITHUB_PATH`: you append a directory, and it's prepended to `PATH` for later steps.

beats.text: GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY: you append Markdown, and it's shown on the run's summary page. The limit is 1 MiB per step, and 20 step summaries are shown per job.
beats.tele: `GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY`: you append Markdown, and it's shown on the run's summary page. The limit is 1 MiB per step, and 20 step summaries are shown per job.

beats.text: Crossing a job boundary. A step output is local to its job. To cross to another job it must be re-exported as a job output, under the outputs key of the job, and read in the other job through the needs context. Two details: an output that looks like a secret is dropped with a message. And multi-line values use a delimiter form.
beats.tele: Crossing a job boundary. A step output is local to its job. To cross to another job it must be re-exported as a job output, under the `outputs` key of the job, and read in the other job through the `needs` context. Two details: an output that looks like a secret is dropped with a message. And multi-line values use a delimiter form.

beats.text: What doesn't cross a job boundary this way: files. Job outputs are strings. Files cross as artifacts, which is video 146.
beats.tele: What doesn't cross a job boundary this way: files. Job outputs are strings. Files cross as artifacts, which is video 146.

beats.text: Older tutorials write outputs with a line that starts with two colons and set-output. That form, and save-state, are deprecated since the eleventh of October 2022. They still work with a warning. The planned removal was postponed on the twenty-fourth of July 2023, and the current workflow commands page no longer documents them. The reason for the change is visible in the form itself: it was a magic line on standard output. So any program whose output a step printed, including a test that echoed untrusted input, could set outputs.
beats.tele: Older tutorials write outputs with a line that starts with two colons and `set-output`. That form, and `save-state`, are deprecated since the eleventh of October 2022. They still work with a warning. The planned removal was postponed on the twenty-fourth of July 2023, and the current workflow commands page no longer documents them. The reason for the change is visible in the form itself: it was a magic line on standard output. So any program whose output a step printed, including a test that echoed untrusted input, could set outputs.

beats.text: Think of a job as a row of sealed rooms along one corridor.
beats.tele: Think of a job as a row of sealed rooms along one corridor.

beats.text: Each run step is a room. A new shell is started in it, your script runs, the shell exits, and the room is cleared: its variables, its current directory, its shell options. What's left is the corridor, which is the runner's filesystem. Files you wrote to disk are still there for the next step.
beats.tele: Each `run` step is a room. A new shell is started in it, your script runs, the shell exits, and the room is cleared: its variables, its current directory, its shell options. What's left is the corridor, which is the runner's filesystem. Files you wrote to disk are still there for the next step.

beats.text: Underneath the rooms runs a pneumatic tube: a small file whose path the runner gives to every step. A step may drop notes into it, one per line, name=value. When the step ends, the runner reads the notes and makes them available to later steps by name.
beats.tele: Underneath the rooms runs a pneumatic tube: a small file whose path the runner gives to every step. A step may drop notes into it, one per line, `name=value`. When the step ends, the runner reads the notes and makes them available to later steps by name.

beats.text: Where the picture breaks: the corridor ends at the job. The next job is in another building, on another machine, and neither the corridor nor the tube reaches it. Only what the job declares at its door, under outputs, is carried over, and only as a string.
beats.tele: Where the picture breaks: the corridor ends at the job. The next job is in another building, on another machine, and neither the corridor nor the tube reaches it. Only what the job declares at its door, under `outputs`, is carried over, and only as a string.

beats.text: The second break concerns the rooms. They aren't all built alike. Whether a room has the pipefail rule depends on a key you may not have written.
beats.tele: The second break concerns the rooms. They aren't all built alike. Whether a room has the `pipefail` rule depends on a key you may not have written.

says: Whether a room has the pipefail rule depends on a key you may not have written

beats.text: Three mechanisms on one picture. Nothing in the shell survives a step. A named value survives through the file. Only a job output leaves the box.
beats.tele: Three mechanisms on one picture. Nothing in the shell survives a step. A named value survives through the file. Only a job output leaves the box.

beats.text: Step 1: the same script, two templates.
beats.tele: Step 1: the same script, two templates.

beats.text: The script has three lines. set -u. Then false piped into tee. Then an echo that says the step reached its last line. false always fails. Under the first template, does the script reach its last line, and what's the exit status? And under the second? Say it out loud.
beats.tele: The script has three lines. `set -u`. Then `false` piped into `tee`. Then an `echo` that says the step reached its last line. `false` always fails. Under the first template, does the script reach its last line, and what's the exit status? And under the second? Say it out loud.

beats.text: Under bash -e, the last line is printed and the exit status is 0. The step would be green, although false failed, because tee succeeded. There's the green failure from the opening. Under the shell: bash template the same script stops with status 1 and never prints the line.
beats.tele: Under `bash -e`, the last line is printed and the exit status is 0. The step would be green, although `false` failed, because `tee` succeeded. There's the green failure from the opening. Under the `shell: bash` template the same script stops with status 1 and never prints the line.

beats.text: This answers the CTO's fourth question. A green job proves only that the last command of every pipeline succeeded, unless the shell was declared.
beats.tele: This answers the CTO's fourth question. A green job proves only that the last command of every pipeline succeeded, unless the shell was declared.

beats.text: Try it now, thirty seconds, in your own terminal. Type false | tee /dev/null, press Enter, then type echo $?. Nothing is written anywhere. Which number do you get?
beats.tele: Try it now, thirty seconds, in your own terminal. Type `false | tee /dev/null`, press Enter, then type `echo $?`. Nothing is written anywhere. Which number do you get?

beats.text: Zero. echo $? prints the exit status of the line before it, and a pipeline reports its last command. tee succeeded, so the failure of false is gone.
beats.tele: Zero. `echo $?` prints the exit status of the line before it, and a pipeline reports its last command. `tee` succeeded, so the failure of `false` is gone.

beats.text: Step 2: a new process per step.
beats.tele: Step 2: a new process per step.

beats.text: The first script exports BUILD_ID, changes into build, and prints the directory. The second prints BUILD_ID and the directory. What does the second script print? Make your prediction.
beats.tele: The first script exports `BUILD_ID`, changes into `build`, and prints the directory. The second prints `BUILD_ID` and the directory. What does the second script print? Make your prediction.

beats.text: BUILD_ID is empty, and the directory is the starting directory again. The export and the cd of the first script didn't reach the second. On a runner the same happens between steps. That's why defaults.run.working-directory and GITHUB_ENV exist.
beats.tele: `BUILD_ID` is empty, and the directory is the starting directory again. The export and the `cd` of the first script didn't reach the second. On a runner the same happens between steps. That's why `defaults.run.working-directory` and `GITHUB_ENV` exist.

beats.text: Step 3: GITHUB_OUTPUT.
beats.tele: Step 3: `GITHUB_OUTPUT`.

beats.text: On a runner the path is given to each step. Here a file in the sandbox stands in for it.
beats.tele: On a runner the path is given to each step. Here a file in the sandbox stands in for it.

beats.text: The file is an append-only list of assignments. Two single-line values first. Then a multi-line value in the delimiter form: the name, two less-than signs and a delimiter word, the lines, and the delimiter word again.
beats.tele: The file is an append-only list of assignments. Two single-line values first. Then a multi-line value in the delimiter form: the name, two less-than signs and a delimiter word, the lines, and the delimiter word again.

beats.text: Two habits, both from the textbook. Always quote the variable. And always use two greater-than signs: a single one discards what earlier lines of the same step wrote.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Piping a test command into tee in a step without a shell key. Root cause: the implicit template is bash -e without pipefail, so the pipeline's status is that of tee.
beats.tele: Piping a test command into `tee` in a step without a `shell` key. Root cause: the implicit template is `bash -e` without `pipefail`, so the pipeline's status is that of `tee`.

beats.text: Setting a variable or changing directory in one step and relying on it in the next. Root cause: each run step is a new shell process.
beats.tele: Setting a variable or changing directory in one step and relying on it in the next. Root cause: each `run` step is a new shell process.

beats.text: Writing to GITHUB_OUTPUT with a single >. Root cause: that truncates the file and discards what earlier lines of the same step wrote.
beats.tele: Writing to `GITHUB_OUTPUT` with a single `>`. Root cause: that truncates the file and discards what earlier lines of the same step wrote.

beats.text: Assuming bash inside a job container. Root cause: the default shell there is sh.
